clue.text: Applied for protection, with no end of trouble

indicators.note: having no end means the final letter of the coating is dropped

parts.note: paint is what gets applied to wood or metal to protect it

explanation.surface: Someone sought protection because of the endless hassle they faced.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Applied for protection' reads as a request for safety, but it describes a coating: PAINT, which loses its last letter T.
explanation.definitionFit: Pain and trouble are both everyday words for distress or bother, so one stands for the other.

clue.text: Having lost bearings, perhaps crashes

indicators.note: a thing that has lost its way is scrambled, so these letters are rearranged

explanation.surface: A disoriented driver, having lost their bearings, crashes.
explanation.walkthrough: 'lost' shuffles BEARINGS into BARGES IN; 'perhaps' marks crashing a party as one way of intruding.
explanation.definitionFit: To crash a party is one example of pushing in uninvited, so 'perhaps' hedges the example.

clue.text: Torn clothing, no end

indicators.note: no here means without, so the word for purpose is removed from the garments

parts.note: raiment is an old word for clothing
an end is a purpose or aim, as in 'to what end?'

explanation.surface: A ripped garment, with no end to its damage.
explanation.walkthrough: 'no end' looks like 'drop the last letter', the theme's usual trick, but here 'end' means purpose: AIM is taken out of RAIMENT.
explanation.definitionFit: Rent is the past tense of rend, to tear, so it means ripped.

clue.text: Rank of copper taking lifer without hesitation in southern Ireland

indicators.note: taking means the police abbreviation holds the rest inside it

parts.note: PC is a police constable, slang copper

indicators.note: in places the shortened prisoner inside the Irish abbreviation

parts.note: ROI is the Republic of Ireland, the southern part of the island

indicators.note: without means the hesitation sound is removed from the prisoner word

parts.note: a lifer is a prisoner serving a life sentence
er is the sound of hesitation

explanation.surface: A policeman arrests a life prisoner in the Irish Republic.
explanation.walkthrough: 'without hesitation' takes ER off the prisoner word, leaving LIF; 'Rank' looks like a grade but means lush and abundant.
explanation.definitionFit: Rank can mean growing thickly and abundantly, as rank weeds do, which is the sense of fruitful and abundant here.

clue.text: No end of obsession over chocolate

indicators.note: in a down entry, over puts the first piece above the second
end of picks the last letter of the word for fixation

parts.note: umber is a brown pigment, and chocolate is a shade of brown

explanation.surface: No end of obsession with chocolate, as any addict knows.
explanation.walkthrough: 'No' looks like part of 'No end', but it is the definition: No. is the standard abbreviation for number.
explanation.definitionFit: The abbreviation No. stands for a numeral or figure, as in 'No. 10'.

clue.text: A pact long held in state where all are happy

parts.note: A as the number one, the Roman I
a deal is an agreement or pact

indicators.note: held in means the size letter is placed inside the verb for declare

parts.note: to word something is to state it
L is the abbreviation for long, as in clothing sizes

explanation.surface: A long-held agreement in a nation where everyone is content.
explanation.walkthrough: 'state' looks like a country but is a verb, WORD, with L held in it.
explanation.definitionFit: A utopia, an imagined perfect place, is somewhere everybody is content.

clue.text: In empty greenhouse, step in muck

indicators.note: In at the start places the ladder piece inside the emptied word
empty removes the inside of the word, leaving only its outer letters

parts.note: a rung is a step on a ladder

explanation.surface: A gardener treads in dirt inside a bare greenhouse.
explanation.walkthrough: 'empty' strips 'greenhouse' to GE, its outer letters; 'In' at the start is the container signal, while the later 'in' is only a link.
explanation.definitionFit: Grunge is grime or dirt, an informal synonym for filth.

clue.text: Animal yelps getting up — get fixed at vet's

indicators.note: in a down entry, getting up means the barks are read from bottom to top

parts.note: yaps are the sharp barks of a small dog

explanation.surface: A yelping pet gets up before being neutered at the vet's.
explanation.definitionFit: To spay a female animal is to neuter it, which is what 'get fixed' means in pet-owner slang.

clue.text: Saw our time span

parts.note: AD, anno domini, is the current era
an age is a span of time

explanation.surface: We saw our time span pass.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Saw' looks like a verb but is the noun for a proverb.
explanation.definitionFit: A saw is an old saying, a proverb, which is what an adage is.

clue.text: A journey with no end of rough caper

parts.note: a round figure is a rough or approximate one
to caper is to skip or trip about

explanation.surface: An endless trek, a wild sort of adventure.
explanation.walkthrough: A journey there and back returns to its start, so on a map it has no end point.
explanation.definitionFit: An outing that comes back to where it began draws a closed loop with no terminus.

clue.text: Disco hit follows appearance in which One Direction turned round?

indicators.note: follows puts the strike word after the altered word

indicators.text: in which One Direction turned round
indicators.note: one compass direction is flipped to its opposite, south becoming north

parts.note: a sight is an appearance or spectacle
to club is to hit

explanation.surface: A pop hit after a show by the boy band One Direction turned the disco round.
explanation.walkthrough: One Direction is a British boy band, but here it is a compass point: S in SIGHT is turned to N.
explanation.definitionFit: A disco is a dance venue, the kind of late-night entertainment spot with music.

clue.text: Article leads to no end of ruddy trouble

parts.note: an is the indefinite article, and it leads, coming first

indicators.note: end of takes the final letter of the colour word

explanation.surface: A newspaper article sparks endless bloody trouble.
explanation.walkthrough: 'ruddy' is British slang for bloody, but only its last letter Y is used.
explanation.definitionFit: To trouble someone is to bother or irritate them.

clue.text: Flag-waving, safe, holding back enemy

indicators.note: holding means the shuffled letters contain the reversed foe
waving means the letters flutter about into a new order
back means the hostile word is read right to left

parts.note: a foe is an enemy

explanation.surface: Flag-waving keeps the country safe, keeping the enemy back.
explanation.walkthrough: SAFE shuffled gives EAS F, holding EOF, which is FOE reversed.
explanation.definitionFit: To flag is to tire or slacken, which is what letting up or relaxing effort means.

clue.text: I won't discuss this theme

parts.note: the phrase said to close a conversation, and also the puzzle's running theme of words without ends

explanation.definitionFit: The idiom ending a subject, 'and that's that', also names the puzzle's recurring device of lopped words.

clue.text: Boatman's glance could be the end of you, they say unfairly

indicators.note: they say signals that the phrase is heard rather than spelt

parts.words: Boatman's glance could be the end of you
parts.note: the setter Boatman refers to himself as one, so his glance is one's eye; something that could kill you is deadly

explanation.surface: The setter's stare could kill, people say, and that is not fair.
explanation.walkthrough: Said aloud, 'one's eye deadly' comes close to the answer.
explanation.definitionFit: Acting with bias toward a single party is acting unjustly.

clue.text: Lack of experience shows in wrong answers

indicators.note: wrong signals the letters are set in a faulty order

explanation.surface: A novice's inexperience is shown by their incorrect answers.
explanation.definitionFit: Someone raw is green and untrained, so the noun is inexperience.

clue.text: See 18
Troubled no end by lover of verse

indicators.note: troubled letters are disturbed into another arrangement

explanation.surface: A poetry fan was endlessly upset.
explanation.walkthrough: John Donne was the English metaphysical poet, famed for his love poems.
explanation.definitionFit: Donne wrote many amorous poems, so he is a poet of love.

clue.text: No end of justice for Spooner? Not today!

indicators.note: Spooner swapped the first sounds of words, so the two words trade openings

parts.note: a place that is shut is not open today
a court is where justice is done

explanation.surface: No justice for the Reverend Spooner: the hearing is off today.
explanation.walkthrough: Swapping the openings of 'shut court' by sound gives the answer; in crosswords a word with no end is one with its last letter cut.
explanation.definitionFit: A word cut off before its final letter literally has no ending.

clue.text: Brass neck acerbity

parts.note: brass is British slang for a prostitute, as is tart
a neck of land is a headland, which is a ness

explanation.surface: Brass neck shows sharpness of tongue.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Brass neck' is British slang for cheek, but here the words split into two separate pieces.
explanation.definitionFit: Acerbity is sourness or sharpness, the quality of being sharp-tasting.

clue.text: After ranger's first greeting, no end of hunting for him?

indicators.note: After puts the greeting behind the first letter
first picks the opening letter of the game warden word

parts.note: hi is a greeting

explanation.surface: A ranger says hello but has no end of hunting for a beast.
explanation.walkthrough: The definition is the quarry a big-game hunter aims at, the end point of the hunt.
explanation.definitionFit: A big horned African beast is a classic target, the goal of a safari hunt.

clue.text: Saki: some rice distilled, having the parts recombined at molecular level

definitions.text: having the parts recombined at molecular level

indicators.note: distilled means drawn out of the words, as spirit is drawn from a mash

explanation.surface: Saki, a spirit distilled from rice, has its molecules rearranged.
explanation.walkthrough: Saki is a pun on sake, the rice wine; the letters sit across 'Saki: some rice'.
explanation.definitionFit: Isomers have the same atoms arranged differently, which is the chemists' word for same-formula compounds.

clue.text: No end of trouble in bingeing and dieting

indicators.note: No means the letter is missing from the gorging word

parts.note: feasting is eating to excess, bingeing

indicators.note: end of takes the final letter of the word for bother

explanation.surface: No end of trouble from bingeing and then dieting.
explanation.walkthrough: FEASTING loses E, the last letter of 'trouble', so the gorging word turns into its opposite.
explanation.definitionFit: Going without food is dieting in the extreme sense.

clue.text: Verse has no end. No end? Odd, in a way

indicators.note: in places the rearranged letters within the road abbreviation

parts.note: ST is the abbreviation for street, a way

indicators.note: odd means strange, so the letters are put in a peculiar order
has no end says the last letter of the following phrase goes

explanation.surface: A poem that never ends: strange, in a way.
explanation.walkthrough: 'has no end' trims 'No end' to NOEN, and 'Odd' shuffles that to ONNE. The theme phrase is used twice: once as an instruction and once as letters.
explanation.definitionFit: A fourteen-line poem is one form of verse.

clue.text: Boring speaker gets up to talk: a low point

indicators.note: in a down entry, gets up means the pieces are read upwards

parts.note: to gab is to chatter
a sag is a part that sinks, a dip or low point

explanation.surface: A dull orator rises to speak, which is a low point.
explanation.walkthrough: GAB then SAG, read from the bottom up, gives the answer.
explanation.definitionFit: A gasbag is a windbag, someone who talks too much and tediously.

clue.text: Cadet or raw soldier?

indicators.note: raw means unrefined, so the letters are in a rough new order

explanation.surface: A cadet or an untrained soldier?
explanation.walkthrough: The question mark admits that a redcoat is an old British soldier and also a holiday-camp entertainer.
explanation.definitionFit: Redcoats were British infantrymen, named for their scarlet tunics.

clue.text: Boatman here: Africa? No end in sight

indicators.note: in sight means visible within the words, spanning them

explanation.surface: The setter Boatman is in Africa, with no end in sight.
explanation.walkthrough: The letters run across 'Africa? No end'.
explanation.definitionFit: A paddler sits in a light boat, so this is the boatman's place.

clue.text: Enquire after report of sea vessel

indicators.note: a report is something heard, so the word is taken by its sound

parts.note: sea is said like the letter C
to ask is to enquire

explanation.surface: Enquire after a report of a ship at sea.
explanation.walkthrough: 'after' places ASK behind the sound of C; 'vessel' looks like a ship but is a container.
explanation.definitionFit: A barrel is a vessel for holding liquid, like beer or wine.

clue.text: With no end in sight, perhaps the French take a boat

parts.note: sight is one of the five senses
le is French for the
SS is a steamship

explanation.surface: Endlessly in view, perhaps the French set off by boat.
explanation.walkthrough: Here 'end' means purpose, so having no end is being pointless.
explanation.definitionFit: Pointless and purposeless things lack an aim, which is what lacking an end means here.

clue.text: Drops of ethanol burn brightly, shining on top

indicators.note: on top in a down entry picks the opening letter of each word

explanation.surface: Drops of ethanol burn brightly with a shine on top.
explanation.definitionFit: When a tide ebbs it falls or recedes, so it drops.

clue.text: Source of starch in the past

definitions.text: Source of starch in the past

indicators.note: the source of a word is its first letter

parts.note: ago means in the past

explanation.surface: A starchy food that was eaten long ago.
explanation.definitionFit: Sago is a starch from the pith of palms, used in old school puddings.

clue.text: No end of trouble from what lorries may do

definitions.meaning: an informal British term for a great many, lots and lots

definitions.text: trouble from what lorries may do
definitions.meaning: trucks that drop their cargo on the road cause chaos

explanation.surface: Endless trouble caused by lorries.
explanation.definitionFit: The British slang for a huge quantity comes from trucks spilling their cargo.

clue.text: Putting together no end of flashy accessories

indicators.note: no means without, so the word for finish is removed

parts.note: blending is mixing or putting together
taken as written

explanation.surface: Assembling a huge stock of showy jewellery.
explanation.walkthrough: 'no end' here removes the word END from BLENDING.
explanation.definitionFit: Bling is showy jewellery and other ostentatious adornments.
